sandhi.note: The m of तम् joins the vowel; the final m of आयान्तम् becomes anusvāra before t; -aḥ before the voiced d becomes -o.
Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra.

samasa.vigraha: सर्वे दैत्यजनाः सर्वदैत्यजनाः; तेषाम् ईश्वरः, तम्
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a karmadhāraya (सर्वदैत्यजन; दैत्यजन itself दैत्याः जनाः, a karmadhāraya)
samasa.literal: the lord of all the Daitya people
samasa.sense: Śumbha, sovereign of the whole Daitya race
samasa.alt: दैत्यजन may also be taken as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, दैत्यानां जनाः, ‘the people of the Daityas’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Present participle of आ + √या (stem आयात्, strong stem आयान्त्), accusative singular: ‘(him) coming on’.
Absolutive of √भिद् ‘to split, pierce’: the root’s d becomes t before -त्वा (खरि च, 8.4.55).
The same causative periphrastic perfect as in 10.20, here with the Goddess as subject: ‘made (him) fall’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देवी आयान्तं सर्वदैत्यजनेश्वरं तं शूलेन वक्षसि भित्त्वा जगत्यां पातयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject देवी, verb पातयामास, object तम् (with आयान्तम् and the epithet), the absolutive phrase शूलेन वक्षसि भित्त्वा, and the locative जगत्याम्.
mantras.lit: Then the Goddess, having pierced him in the chest with her trident, felled him, the lord of all the Daitya people, as he was coming on, upon the earth.
mantras.tr: Then, as the lord of all the Daityas came at her, the Goddess pierced his chest with her trident and struck him down to the earth.

comm.t: The death blow. After the weapons, the sky-fight and the wrestling, the Goddess ends the battle with her trident (शूल) through his chest, as she ended Niśumbha’s with a trident-blow to the heart (9.34).

A modern reading: the epithet given at the moment of death — ‘lord of all the Daitya people’ — states what falls with him. The king is the last of his army; with him the whole order of the asuras ends.

samasa.vigraha: देव्याः शूलम् देवीशूलम्; तस्य अग्रम् देवीशूलाग्रम्; तेन विक्षतः
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing two ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas (देवीशूल, देवीशूलाग्र)
samasa.literal: torn by the tip of the Goddess’s trident
samasa.sense: pierced through by her trident’s point

samasa.vigraha: अब्धयः च द्वीपाः च अब्धिद्वीपाः; अब्धिद्वीपैः सह वर्तमाना, ताम्
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (with स- for सह) containing an itaretara dvandva (अब्धिद्वीप)
samasa.literal: (the earth) that is together with oceans and islands
samasa.sense: the earth with all its seas and continents

samasa.literal: (the earth) that is together with mountains

morph.note: Present participle of the causative of √चल् ‘to move’: ‘causing to move’, i.e. shaking. Nominative singular masculine, agreeing with सः.
Masculine nominative of the u-stem compound; असु ‘life-breath’ is used in the plural (असवः), hence गताः असवः.

mantras.anvaya: देवीशूलाग्रविक्षतः गतासुः सः साब्धिद्वीपां सपर्वतां सकलां पृथ्वीं चालयन् उर्व्यां पपात।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject सः with two qualifiers (गतासुः, देवीशूलाग्रविक्षतः), verb पपात with the locative उर्व्याम्, and the participial phrase चालयन् … पृथ्वीम् with its three qualifiers.
mantras.lit: He, lifeless, wounded by the point of the Goddess’s trident, fell on the earth, shaking the whole earth with its oceans and continents, with its mountains.
mantras.tr: Pierced by the point of the Goddess’s trident, he fell lifeless to the ground, and the whole earth shook — its oceans, its continents and its mountains.

comm.t: Śumbha dies. His fall shakes the whole earth — a measure of his size and power, and of the scale of what has been overcome.
With Śumbha’s death the third carita’s battle is over. In the Gita Press pāṭha the next chapter (11) is the gods’ hymn to Nārāyaṇī, sung in thanksgiving.

samasa.literal: in him whose self is bad

morph.note: Perfect of √आप्: the reduplicated आ + आप् merge into आप (third singular). ‘Attained’.
Locative absolute (हते तस्मिन् दुरात्मनि): ‘that wicked one having been slain’ — the circumstance of the whole verse.

mantras.anvaya: ततः तस्मिन् दुरात्मनि हते, अखिलं जगत् प्रसन्नम् (सत्) अतीव स्वास्थ्यम् आप, नभः च निर्मलम् अभवत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (हते तस्मिन् दुरात्मनि) and two clauses: जगत् (with प्रसन्नम्, अखिलम्) स्वास्थ्यम् आप, and नभः निर्मलम् अभवत्.
mantras.lit: Then, that evil-souled one having been slain, the whole world, become serene, attained exceeding well-being, and the sky became stainless.
mantras.tr: When that wicked one was slain, the whole world grew serene and was restored to perfect health, and the sky became clear.

comm.t: The cosmic consequence of the victory: the world (जगत्) recovers its health, and the sky clears. Verses 10.28–32 describe the return of order in nature.
A modern reading: स्वास्थ्य, ‘health’, is literally ‘being established in oneself’. The verse pictures the world, freed of oppression, returning to its own nature.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (madhyama-pada-lopin: the middle word ‘indicating’ is dropped)
samasa.alt: Also a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, उत्पातस्य मेघाः, ‘clouds of calamity’; the sense is the same.

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (वाहिन्, √वह् + णिनि, ‘habitually flowing’; feminine वाहिनी)

morph.note: Imperfect plural of √अस्, used twice: of the clouds that ‘were’ before, and of the rivers that ‘became’ again what they should be.
Locative absolute with the causative participle पातित, ‘(he) having been made to fall’. The subject (तस्मिन्) is understood from 10.28.

mantras.anvaya: प्राक् ये सोल्काः उत्पातमेघाः आसन्, ते शमं ययुः। तत्र (तस्मिन्) पातिते सरितः तथा मार्गवाहिन्यः आसन्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative-correlative sentence (ये … आसन्, ते शमं ययुः) and a second sentence with a locative absolute (तत्र पातिते).
mantras.lit: The portent-clouds, with meteors, which had been before — they went to calm. When (he) had been felled there, the rivers likewise became flowing in their courses.
mantras.tr: The ominous clouds and falling meteors that had been seen before all vanished, and once he had fallen, the rivers flowed again within their banks.
mantras.tr_note: ‘within their banks’ interprets मार्गवाहिन्यः, ‘flowing by (their) course’.

comm.t: The signs of disorder disappear: the ominous clouds and meteors that had accompanied the asura reign subside, and the rivers return to their beds.

The gods will ask in their hymn (11.34) that the Goddess quell ‘the great calamities born of the ripening of portents’ (उत्पातपाकजनितान् … महोपसर्गान्). The vocabulary of portents in this verse anticipates that prayer.
